newsitem.title: UK: Dollar drifts up in late Europe, poised for FOMC.
newsitem.headline: Dollar drifts up in late Europe, poised for FOMC.

text.p: The dollar firmed to its session high against the mark by late European trade, with short-covering kicking in ahead of the Federal Reserve's policy-making meeting on Tuesday.
Dollar/mark was boosted also because the mark was pressured by a Bundesbank council member's comments on Germany's efforts to meet the criteria for European monetary union, traders said.
"The dollar's been gaining on short-covering, particularly against the mark, although against the yen there seems to be quite a lot of offers above 116.30," said a trader at a U.S. bank in London.
"The Bundesbank comments are not helping the case for the mark, either," the trader said.
The dollar was at 1.7104/07 marks at 1520 GMT, just off its session high and up from 1.6900/10 in late Europe on Friday.
It was at 116.22/32 yen against 115.32/37 on Friday, recovering from the beating it suffered overnight from a larger-than-expected rise in Japan's trade surplus.

Analysts expected the dollar to tread water against the mark and yen ahead of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting scheduled on Tuesday, adding that the issue of a rate hike was still a very close call.

"Many are looking for a 25-basis-point hike (in the federal funds rate) and if this doesn't happen there might be some disappointment... but we're pretty well settled in the 1.70-mark area for now," said Claudio Demolli, foreign exchange analyst at Merrill Lynch in London.

The U.S. bank trader, noting that dollar/mark had been repeatedly rebuffed by resistance at around 1.71 in recent days, said a clear breach of this level was needed for the dollar to gain substantially.
The continued slide in mark/yen, which fell to its lowest since mid-September 1995, was also supporting dollar/mark.
The mark slid to a low of 68.03 yen, compared with late Friday's level of 68.33 yen.
Bundesbank council member Edgar Meister's comment warning about Germany's efforts to meet the EMU criteria, meanwhile, served to dampen the mark against the dollar.

Referring to Germany's estimated tax revenue shortfall of 18 billion marks and Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to reassess the Bundesbank's gold reserves at a higher value closer to market prices, Meister said this showed how "thorny" EMU qualification was for Germany as well.

Meister said Germany's efforts to meet the budget deficit-to-GDP ratio of three percent would now be very closely scrutinised, adding that accounting tricks and short-term measures would undermine trust.

Analysts said such comments were mark-negative because it made the market assume Europe would push ahead with EMU with watered-down criteria and a larger number of members, which would likely result in a weak single currency.
"Fudging the criteria was not something the market was expecting of Germany," Merrill's Demolli said. "The basic idea here is that the wider EMU is, the worse it is for the mark."
"You can't see much difference any more between the core (EMU) countries and the fringe countries, because they are all in the same situation," he said.

On the European crosses, the lira gained on expectations of a rate cut in the near future as the Bank of Italy cut its repo rate today to a historic low of 6.78 percent. Mark/lira was at 981.00/25 against its Friday level of 986.90/7.20.
Sterling was strong on the mark, pulled up by dollar/mark strength and by better-than-expected UK public sector debt data. The pound was steady against the dollar.
-- Chizu Nomiyama, London Forex Desk, +44-171-542-6721
